lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance Schedules
lessons.body:
Preventive maintenance means fixing small problems before they stop your mill. In Africa, most mill breakdowns happen because nobody checked the machine. A simple schedule saves you money and time. Start with a daily checklist: before starting, check oil levels in the gearbox and bearings. Look for loose bolts on the frame and motor. Listen for unusual noise. After milling, clean the machine: remove husk and bran from screens, rollers, and belts. Use a brush and compressed air if available. This takes 15 minutes but prevents rust and clogging.

Weekly tasks: grease all bearings with a grease gun. Check belt tension â press the belt midway; it should deflect about 1 cm. If too loose, tighten. Inspect rubber rollers for wear â if grooves are less than 1 mm deep, plan to replace them. Check the huller blades for dullness. Sharpen or replace if they don't cut cleanly. Also check the separator screens for holes or tears.

Monthly: change oil in the gearbox if you run the mill more than 8 hours a day. Use SAE 90 gear oil. Check alignment of the motor and main shaft with a straight edge â misalignment causes vibration and bearing failure. Inspect all electrical connections for looseness or burning. Tighten terminal screws. Clean the motor cooling fan.

Yearly: replace all belts, bearings, and rubber rollers as a set, even if they look okay. Overhaul the huller and polisher. Replace worn shafts. This costs money but prevents unexpected breakdown during harvest season when you need the mill most.

Keep a logbook. Write down every maintenance action and the date. If you notice a part wearing faster than expected, investigate why â maybe the feed rate is too high or the paddy is too wet. A good schedule turns maintenance from a crisis into a routine. Train one person to be responsible for daily checks. In many African mills, a wall chart with pictures helps workers remember steps. For example, draw a grease gun, a belt, and a roller. Tick each day. This simple system can double the life of your machine.

lessons.title: Common Milling Machine Faults and Repairs
lessons.body:
When your mill stops working, don't panic. Most faults have simple causes. Here are the common ones and how to fix them. First, the mill won't start. Check the power supply: is there electricity? Test with a multimeter. If power is okay, check the circuit breaker â reset it. If it trips again, there's a short circuit. Look for burnt wires or a faulty motor. If the motor hums but doesn't turn, the capacitor may be bad. Replace it with the same microfarad rating. In rural areas, low voltage is common â use a voltage stabilizer if needed.

Second, the mill runs but no rice comes out. This often means the feed gate is closed or blocked. Open the gate and clear any jam. If the paddy is too wet, it sticks and blocks the chute. Dry paddy to 14% moisture before milling. Also check the huller â if the rubber rollers are worn, they won't grip the paddy. Replace them.

Third, excessive vibration. Stop the machine immediately. Check for loose foundation bolts â tighten them. If vibration continues, the main shaft may be bent or the bearings worn. Replace bearings. Also check for unbalanced pulley â a chipped pulley causes vibration. Replace it.

Fourth, rice breaks too much. This is a common complaint. Causes: roller gap too tight, roller speed too high, or paddy too dry. Adjust the roller gap â for most mills, a gap of 0.5 to 1 mm is good. Reduce engine speed if possible. If paddy is below 12% moisture, it becomes brittle. Add moisture by soaking? No â better to harvest at right time.

Fifth, the mill overheats. Check lubrication â dry bearings overheat. Grease them. Also check if the cooling fan is working. Clean dust from the motor. If the mill is overloaded, feed less paddy per minute.

Sixth, unusual noise. A knocking sound means a loose part â tighten all bolts. A squealing sound means a dry or worn bearing â replace it. A grinding sound means metal rubbing â stop and inspect.

For repairs, you need basic tools: spanners, screwdrivers, pliers, a hammer, and a set of Allen keys. Keep spare parts: bearings, belts, rubber rollers, and fuses. In Africa, many millers wait for a technician from town â that can take days. Learn to do minor repairs yourself. If a part is broken and you can't fix it, call a qualified technician. Never put your hand inside a running machine. Always switch off and unplug before repairing. With practice, you can fix 80% of faults in under an hour.

lessons.title: Replacement of Worn Parts (Rollers, Screens)
lessons.body:
Worn parts reduce milling efficiency and quality. Rubber rollers and screens are the most common wear items. Replacing them is a skill every miller should learn. First, when to replace rollers: check the grooves. New rollers have deep grooves (about 2-3 mm). When the grooves are less than 1 mm, or the rubber is smooth, replace them. Also, if rice breakage increases or husking efficiency drops below 90%, it's time. Rollers usually last 800 to 1,200 hours of operation. In Africa, with dusty conditions, they may wear faster. Keep a spare pair.

To replace rollers: switch off and lock out power. Remove the belt guard. Loosen the tensioner and remove the drive belt. Take off the feed hopper. You will see two rollers: one fixed, one adjustable. Remove the bolts holding the bearing caps. Slide out the old roller. Clean the shaft and bearing housing. Inspect bearings â if they are rough or noisy, replace them too. Slide the new roller onto the shaft. Make sure the keyway aligns. Tighten the bearing caps evenly. Adjust the gap between rollers to 0.5-1 mm using a feeler gauge. Turn the rollers by hand to check for smooth rotation. Reassemble in reverse order. Run the mill empty for 2 minutes to check for vibration.

Screens: The screen separates broken rice from whole grain. Holes get clogged or torn. A torn screen lets broken rice mix with whole rice, lowering grade. Replace screens when you see tears or when more than 5% broken rice passes through. To replace: remove the screen frame. Note how it sits â take a photo. Remove old screen. Clean the frame. Install new screen â usually a perforated metal sheet or wire mesh. Secure with clamps or bolts. Ensure it is tight â loose screens vibrate and tear. The screen size depends on rice type: for long grain, use 1.8-2.0 mm holes; for short grain, 1.5-1.6 mm.

Other worn parts: belts (replace when cracked or glazed), bearings (replace when noisy or hot), and huller blades (sharpen or replace when dull). Always use original or high-quality spare parts. Cheap parts fail quickly. In many African markets, counterfeit bearings are common â buy from a trusted supplier. Keep a record of when you replace each part. This helps you predict future replacements. With practice, replacing rollers takes 1 hour; screens take 30 minutes. Doing it yourself saves money and downtime.

lessons.title: Lubrication and Alignment Procedures
lessons.body:
Lubrication and alignment keep your mill running smoothly. Without them, bearings fail, belts wear out, and energy consumption rises. Start with lubrication. Use the right grease and oil. For bearings, use lithium-based grease (NLGI 2). For gearboxes, use SAE 90 gear oil. For chains, use chain oil. Never mix different greases â they can react and lose effectiveness.

How to lubricate: clean the grease fitting with a rag before attaching the grease gun. Pump grease until you see old grease coming out of the bearing seal. That means fresh grease has pushed out the old. Wipe off excess. Do this weekly or every 50 hours of operation. For gearboxes, check oil level daily with the dipstick. Top up if below the mark. Change oil every 500 hours or every 3 months, whichever comes first. Drain oil while warm â it flows better and carries away dirt. Refill with the correct amount â usually 1 to 2 liters for small mills.

Alignment: Misalignment between the motor and the main shaft causes vibration, bearing failure, and belt wear. Check alignment with a straight edge or a laser alignment tool. For most African mills, a straight edge (a steel ruler) works. Place it across the motor pulley and the main pulley. There should be no gap. If there is a gap, adjust the motor position. Loosen the motor mounting bolts. Tap the motor gently with a rubber mallet until the straight edge touches both pulleys evenly. Tighten bolts. Recheck. Also check pulley alignment â the belts should run in a straight line. If belts are misaligned, they wear quickly and may jump off.

Belt tension: Correct tension is critical. Press the belt midway between pulleys. It should deflect about 1 cm (10 mm) for a V-belt. If more, tighten. If less, loosen â too tight damages bearings. Use a belt tension gauge if available. Otherwise, use your thumb.

Shaft alignment: For the main shaft, check runout with a dial indicator. If runout exceeds 0.05 mm, the shaft is bent â replace it. Also check coupling alignment if the mill has one. Use a feeler gauge to check gap at four points (top, bottom, left, right). Adjust shims until gaps are equal.

After alignment, run the mill empty for 10 minutes. Listen for unusual noise. Check for vibration by placing your hand on the bearing housing â it should be warm, not hot. If hot, stop and recheck. Proper lubrication and alignment reduce downtime by 50% and extend bearing life by years. Train one person to do these tasks. Keep a log of when you lubricate and align. In dusty African conditions, do it more often â every 30 hours instead of 50.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Low Milling Yield
lessons.body:
Low milling yield means you get less rice from the same amount of paddy. For example, you expect 65 kg of milled rice from 100 kg paddy, but you get only 50 kg. This is a big loss. Let's find the causes and fixes. First, check paddy quality. If paddy is too wet (above 14% moisture), it sticks to rollers and screens, causing loss. Dry it to 14%. If too dry (below 12%), grains break easily. Soak? No â harvest at right maturity. Also, remove stones, mud, and immature grains before milling. Use a pre-cleaner.

Second, check the huller. Worn rubber rollers don't grip paddy well, so some paddy passes through without being husked. That unhusked paddy goes to the polisher and is lost as bran or broken. Replace rollers when grooves are shallow. Also, set the roller gap correctly â 0.5 to 1 mm. Too wide, no husking; too narrow, breakage.

Third, check the polisher. If the polisher is overworking, it removes too much bran, reducing yield. Adjust the pressure â less pressure means less bran removal. Also, check the screen in the polisher â if clogged, rice stays too long and breaks. Clean screens daily.

Fourth, check the separator. A worn or wrong-sized screen lets good rice go to the bran bin. For example, if screen holes are too large, whole rice falls through. Use the correct screen size: 1.8-2.0 mm for long grain. Also, check the aspiration â too much air blows away good rice. Reduce air speed.

Fifth, check feed rate. Feeding too fast overloads the mill, causing breakage and poor separation. Feed slowly and steadily. The ammeter should read about 80% of full load. If it's at 100%, reduce feed.

Sixth, check machine settings. The clearance between the huller and polisher, the angle of the separator, and the speed of the aspirator all affect yield. Read the manual. If no manual, experiment: change one setting at a time and measure yield. Keep records.

Seventh, maintenance. Worn bearings cause vibration, which breaks rice. Misaligned belts reduce speed. Lubricate and align regularly.

To measure yield, weigh 100 kg paddy. Mill it. Weigh milled rice. Calculate: (milled rice weight / 100) x 100%. Good mills get 65-68%. If below 60%, investigate. Common quick fixes: replace rollers, clean screens, adjust feed, and dry paddy. In Africa, many millers blame the paddy, but often it's the machine. With proper troubleshooting, you can increase yield by 10% or more. That's extra income for you.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Maintenance Logs
lessons.body:
Record keeping is not paperwork for its own sake. It saves you money. A simple logbook tells you when you last changed oil, how much rice you milled, and what repairs you did. Without records, you repeat mistakes and forget maintenance. Start with a notebook and a pen. If you can use a smartphone, use a simple spreadsheet app. But paper works fine.

What to record daily: date, hours run, paddy milled (kg), milled rice produced (kg), and any breakdowns. Also record fuel or electricity used. This helps you calculate cost per kg and profit. At the end of the day, write down any unusual noise, vibration, or smell. If you noticed a loose bolt, write it down and fix it.

Weekly: record maintenance done â greasing, belt tension check, cleaning. Note the condition of rollers, screens, and belts. For example, 'Rollers: grooves 1.5 mm, okay.' 'Screen: small tear, replace next week.' This helps you plan.

Monthly: record oil changes, alignment checks, and parts replaced. Note the cost of parts and labor. Also record yield: (milled rice / paddy) x 100. If yield drops, look back at records to see what changed. Maybe you changed a setting or used different paddy.

Yearly: summarize. How many hours did the mill run? How many breakdowns? What was the total maintenance cost? Which parts wore out fastest? This helps you budget for next year.

Keep a separate log for each machine if you have more than one. Use a table with columns: Date, Hours, Maintenance Done, Parts Used, Cost, Remarks. For example:

| Date | Hours | Maintenance | Parts | Cost | Remarks |
| 1/6 | 8 | Greased bearings | Grease | 500 | Normal |
| 2/6 | 10 | Replaced roller | Roller | 20000 | Grooves worn |

At the end of each month, review the log. Ask: Did I do all scheduled maintenance? If not, why? What can I improve? In Africa, many millers keep records in their head, but that fails when you have many workers. Train one person to be the record keeper. Keep the logbook near the mill, not in an office. Use a wall chart for daily checks â workers tick boxes.

Records also help when you sell the mill â a buyer pays more for a well-maintained machine with logs. And if you apply for a loan, records show you are serious. Start today. Even a simple exercise book is enough. The goal is to know your machine's history so you can predict and prevent problems.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a preventive maintenance schedule?
options: A) To fix breakdowns after they happen
B) To avoid breakdowns by doing regular checks
C) To increase the price of the mill
D) To replace all parts every month
quiz.explanation: Preventive maintenance aims to stop problems before they cause breakdowns.

quiz.q: How often should you grease the bearings on a rice mill?
quiz.explanation: Weekly greasing is recommended for most rice mills, or every 50 hours.

quiz.q: What should you check daily before starting the mill?
options: A) Oil levels and loose bolts
quiz.explanation: Daily checks include oil levels, loose bolts, and unusual noise.

quiz.q: What is a sign that rubber rollers need replacement?
options: B) Grooves are less than 1 mm deep
quiz.explanation: When grooves wear down to less than 1 mm, husking efficiency drops.

quiz.q: What should you do if the mill motor hums but does not turn?
quiz.explanation: A faulty capacitor is a common cause of a humming motor that won't start.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of excessive vibration in a rice mill?
quiz.explanation: Loose foundation bolts allow the machine to vibrate excessively.

quiz.q: What should you do before repairing any part of the mill?
options: A) Switch off and unplug power
quiz.explanation: Always lock out power to prevent accidental start-up during repairs.

quiz.q: How long do rubber rollers typically last?
quiz.explanation: Under normal conditions, rubber rollers last about 800 to 1,200 hours.

quiz.q: What is the correct roller gap for most rice mills?
quiz.explanation: A gap of 0.5 to 1 mm provides good husking without breakage.

quiz.q: When should you replace a screen in the rice mill?
options: B) When it has tears or holes
quiz.explanation: Tears or holes let broken rice mix with whole rice, reducing grade.

quiz.q: What type of grease is recommended for rice mill bearings?
quiz.explanation: Lithium-based grease (NLGI 2) is suitable for high-speed bearings.

quiz.q: How often should you change gearbox oil?
quiz.explanation: Regular oil changes prevent wear and overheating.

quiz.q: What is the correct belt tension for a V-belt?
quiz.explanation: A deflection of about 1 cm indicates correct tension.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to check alignment of pulleys?
quiz.explanation: A straight edge placed across pulleys shows misalignment.

quiz.q: What is a sign of misalignment in a rice mill?
quiz.explanation: Misalignment causes vibration and rapid belt wear.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for paddy before milling?
quiz.explanation: 14% moisture is ideal; too wet or too dry causes breakage.

quiz.q: What causes low milling yield due to the huller?
quiz.explanation: Worn rollers don't grip paddy, so some pass through unhusked.

quiz.q: What should you do if the polisher removes too much bran?
quiz.explanation: Reducing polisher pressure prevents excessive bran removal.

quiz.q: What is a good milling yield percentage for rice?
quiz.explanation: A well-maintained mill should achieve 65-68% yield.

quiz.q: What should you record daily in a maintenance log?
options: B) Hours run, paddy milled, and any issues
quiz.explanation: Daily records help track performance and spot problems early.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for a rice mill?
options: A) It helps predict and prevent problems
B) It increases the mill's speed
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Records show patterns that help you plan maintenance and improve yield.

quiz.q: What should you do before attaching a grease gun to a fitting?
options: A) Clean the fitting with a rag
quiz.explanation: Cleaning prevents dirt from entering the bearing.

quiz.q: What is the correct screen size for long grain rice?
quiz.explanation: Long grain rice requires larger holes (1.8-2.0 mm) to prevent loss.

quiz.q: What should you do if you notice a knocking sound from the mill?
options: B) Stop and tighten loose parts
quiz.explanation: Knocking indicates loose parts; stop and tighten them.

quiz.q: How often should you check belt tension?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks ensure belts are not too loose or too tight.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of low yield when paddy is too dry?
quiz.explanation: Too dry paddy becomes brittle and breaks easily during milling.

quiz.q: What should you do if the mill overheats?
quiz.explanation: Overheating often results from dry bearings or blocked cooling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a maintenance log?
options: A) To record daily activities and plan repairs
B) To replace the need for maintenance
C) To show off to customers
quiz.explanation: A log helps you track maintenance and predict future needs.

quiz.q: What should you do before replacing a roller?
quiz.explanation: Always lock out power to prevent injury during roller replacement.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a worn bearing?
quiz.explanation: Worn bearings make noise and run hot.
